sections.title: How does the Chain length calculator work?
sections.html:
The Chain length calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports chain stay length in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the largest front chainring, the chain length and the shortest possible chain length.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Chain length calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Chain stay length=(1 ÷ 2) × chain length − 1 ÷ 8 × largest front chainring − 1 ÷ 8 × largest rear cog − 1 ÷ 2
Number of links=rounded up, (2 × chain length)
Number of links in shortest possible chain=rounded up, (2 × shortest possible chain length)
Chain stay length=(1 ÷ 5000) × the square root of ((227 × largest front chainring + 1023 × largest rear cog − 2500 × shortest possible chain length) × (1023 × largest front chainring + 227 × largest rear cog − 2500 × shortest possible chain length))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Largest front chainring = 10, Largest rear cog = 10 and Chain length = 30 in. The calculator returns Chain stay length = -285 in, Number of links = 1, Shortest possible chain length = 1070 in and Number of links in shortest possible chain = 22.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Chain stay length = -285 in, Number of links = 1, Shortest possible chain length = 1070 in and Number of links in shortest possible chain = 22 should be roughly the size you expected from Largest front chainring = 10 and Largest rear cog = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Chain length calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the largest front chainring, the chain length and the shortest possible chain length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Chain length calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns chain stay length, derived from the largest front chainring, the chain length and the shortest possible chain length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Chain length calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the largest front chainring, the chain length and the shortest possible chain length, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter chain stay length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Chain stay length opens in inches and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Chain stay length = -285 in. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Chain length calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
